---
title: "4i / cyclic IF"
---

Cyclic immunofluorescence (4i) images the same plate several times, stripping
and re-staining between rounds. That multiplies the number of markers you can
measure per cell far beyond the three or four channels a single round allows —
but only if the rounds can be registered accurately enough to say that a
nucleus in round 3 is the *same* nucleus as in round 1.

OMERO-Screen treats each round as an ordinary plate, analysed independently,
and then aligns and merges them afterwards. Four command-line tools do this.

::: {.callout-note}
Detailed wet-lab protocols for the stripping and re-staining rounds are being
prepared and will be added here. This page covers the computational side.
:::

## The workflow

| Step | Tool | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `omero-screen` | Analyse **each round** as a normal plate |
| 2 | `align_plates.py` | Register the rounds against a reference plate |
| 3 | `create_masks.py` | Fill in cell masks missing from secondary rounds |
| 4 | `aggregate_plates.py` | Merge per-cell features across rounds |
| 5 | `alignment_qc.py` | Check the registration actually worked |

The first plate you pass to `align_plates.py` is the **reference**; every other
round is registered onto it, and the aggregated dataset carries its plate ID.

::: {.callout-warning}
These are `bin/` utilities and still use argparse, unlike the four main
commands. That means they keep argparse conventions — including abbreviated
options — and they are run with `python bin/<name>.py` rather than as installed
commands.
:::

## 1. Analyse each round

Run the pipeline on every round separately, exactly as for a single-round
experiment:

```bash
uv run omero-screen 4126 --stitch
uv run omero-screen 4127 --stitch
uv run omero-screen 4128 --stitch
```

Each round gets its own segmentation, features and QC. Nothing at this stage
knows the rounds are related.

## 2. Align the rounds

```bash
python bin/align_plates.py 4126 4127 4128 [options]
```

The first ID is the reference. Alignment is computed on a nuclear channel —
DAPI by default, since it is present in every round and does not move.

| Option | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--channel NAME` | `DAPI` | Channel used for registration |
| `-n N` | 5 | Number of alignments averaged |
| `--sample-alignments` | off | Per-sample alignments instead of a fixed number |
| `--threshold N` | 100 | Distance threshold for accepting an alignment |
| `--tolerance N` | 10 | Allowed distance from the alignment centroid |
| `--iqr N` | 1.5 | Inter-quartile-range factor for outlier removal (0 disables) |
| `--gallery N` | 4 | Size of the alignment gallery grid |
| `--seed N` | random | Random seed for sampling |
| `--env NAME` | — | Environment file to load |

## 3. Create missing masks

Secondary rounds are often segmented on the nucleus alone, so they lack cell
masks. This regenerates them from the aligned reference:

```bash
python bin/create_masks.py 4127
```

| Option | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--sample-alignments` | off | Use per-sample rather than per-well alignments |
| `--force` | off | Replace masks that already exist |
| `--env NAME` | — | Environment file to load |

`--sample-alignments` must match how you ran step 2 and how you will run
step 4 — mixing per-sample and per-well alignments produces silently wrong
mappings.

## 4. Aggregate the rounds

```bash
python bin/aggregate_plates.py 4126
```

Pass the **reference** plate ID. Each cell in the reference is matched to its
counterpart in every other round, and their features are merged into one
single-cell table.

| Option | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--method {0,1,2,3}` | 3 | Matching strategy — see below |
| `--threshold N` | 25 | Distance threshold for accepting a mapping |
| `--std N` | 6 | Standard deviations from the mean distance before exclusion |
| `--gallery N` | 4 | Size of the mapping gallery grid |
| `--sample-alignments` | off | Use per-sample rather than per-well alignments |
| `--seed N` | random | Random seed for sampling |
| `--env NAME` | — | Environment file to load |

**Matching methods.** `0` minimum distance; `1` KD-tree minimum distance;
`2` greedy nearest neighbour; `3` mask overlap. The default, mask overlap, is
the most conservative: it requires the two nuclei to physically overlap rather
than merely being closest, which is what you want when cells may have moved
slightly between rounds.

## 5. Check the alignment

Registration failure is the main risk in a 4i experiment, and it is not always
visible in the final plot. Run the QC report before trusting the data:

```bash
python bin/alignment_qc.py 4126 -o alignment_qc
```

Pass several master plate IDs to treat them as biological replicates and get a
combined, replicate-level analysis.

| Option | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `-o, --outdir DIR` | `alignment_qc` | Destination for CSVs, tables and figures |
| `--sample-alignments` | off | Must match how `aggregate_plates` was run |
| `--iqr N` | 1.5 | IQR factor for per-well agreement outlier removal |
| `--mask-samples N` | 12 | Fields sampled for nuclear-mask overlap (0 to skip) |
| `--pixel-size N` | — | Override the pixel size |
| `--attach` | — | Attach the report back to the OMERO plate |
| `--seed N` | random | Random seed for sampling |
| `--env NAME` | — | Environment file to load |

The report collects the raw input CSVs, derived metric tables, summary
statistics and figures in one directory, so it can be archived alongside the
analysis.

## Then what

The aggregated plate behaves like any other from here: import it with
`cellview import plate <reference_id>` and plot it with the usual functions.
Each cell now carries the features from every round.

::: {.callout-note}
**A known caveat.** Nuclei with no matching cell mask are dropped during the
merge rather than carried through with null features. The loss concentrates at
canvas borders, where cells are more likely to be clipped than nuclei, so raw
counts near the edge of an imaged region are biased slightly downwards.
:::
